fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Spent Mushroom Blocks Become Garden Soil", "body": "Frosch describes Family Fungi as a mushroom farm whose most valuable output is not the mushrooms but the spent mycelium blocks left after one or two flushes, which stop being commercially viable once they take up shelf space. He drives 25 to 30 minutes to a local sawmill, takes the hardwood waste stream from lumber headed into people's houses, grows it out, then returns it to the ground. In South Louisiana, with its very high water table and heavy clay, he says the blocks need about eight months to break down into something he compares to rich Dutch chocolate cake, and stacked in thirties they keep fruiting in the garden."}, {"title": "Quantity Farming Versus Qualitative Nourishment", "body": "Garton argues that people treat food like putting gas in a car, judging only whether the tank is full, while Frosch calls boxed products food stuff: made from food, but no longer food. Frosch says he takes issue with organic labeling loopholes, observes that hurricane shelves empty first of pop tarts and beer, and estimates his family produces roughly 20 percent of its calories from about a quarter acre of intensive perennial and mixed annual planting on their four acres. Garton frames industrialization as a genuine answer to an old problem, feeding everyone, that has now produced a new one worth tackling."}, {"title": "Where A Beginner Should Start With Fungi", "body": "Asked what a novice should cultivate, Frosch names oyster mushrooms first: easy at home from a grow kit or from spawn on hardwood sawdust, expandable into fresh wood chips or freshly cut logs, widely available and forgiving of neglect. He puts reishi second, grown on a countertop, harvested fresh and dehydrated for tea, or extracted in neutral spirits such as vodka or brandy, with the 190 proof organic alcohol his farm uses as one option and a charcoal filter recommended for vodka. Third is king stropharia, the wine cap or garden giant, which he says will only fruit with soil organisms and a casing layer."}, {"title": "Soil As A Living Sub Aquatic System", "body": "Frosch separates saprotrophic fungi that break down hardwood from mycorrhizal fungi that partner with tree roots, calling the latter the unsung heroes of the food chain for extending root systems enormously and mining minerals with acids like oxalic acid that plants cannot produce. He cites a line he heard from Matt Powers and John Kempf that soil is a sub aquatic system, roughly 20,000 gallons of water per acre in the first foot. He also reports that oyster mushrooms can remediate nematodes, which cause the root knot that once cost him a whole sweet potato harvest."}, {"title": "Weeds, Books And Permission To Start", "body": "Frosch's land was a strawberry plantation 60 to 70 years ago and pine forest savanna before that, and he says it was strip mined for minerals, so he now reads weeds like thistle as indicators of deficiency, uses no herbicides, and mulches or does a chop and drop instead. For study he points to the Louisiana Herb Journal, Matt Powers on regenerative soil, John Kempf on bio fertilizers, and Masanobu Fukuoka's One Straw Revolution and The Natural Way of Farming. He describes the great mother tea his wife Elise first blended for herself, warns against expert-itis, and says a few pots on a balcony is enough to begin."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: James Frosch of Family Fungi joins InnerVerse to explore the healing power of regenerative living, from mushrooms and medicinal herbs to intuitive gardening and the sacred relationship between soil, spirit, and self.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: We talk about the real work of sovereignty, the magic of spent mycelium, and how healing doesn't come in a bottle, it grows from the land beneath your feet.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Medicinal Herb Garden as Entry Point", "body": "James walks through why a small medicinal herb garden is the easiest way to start growing, since culinary herbs like oregano and basil already carry medicinal value. He points to strictly regional resources like the Louisiana Herb Journal and Strictly Medicinal Seeds, and recommends ordering seed in winter for spring planting. He singles out plantain and yarrow as the lowest maintenance allies, both prized for cuts, scrapes and wound healing, plantain even doubling as a balm ingredient. Blue vervain and chickweed round out his beginner list, the first calming nervous tension, the second feeding both people and chickens each February."}, {"title": "Plant Signatures From Mugwort to Alliums", "body": "Beyond nutrition, James reads specific plants through their signatures and folklore. Mugwort, a onetime beer ingredient before purity laws standardized hops and barley, gets grown as a protective dream herb. Alliums like Egyptian walking onions and chives earn a permanent spot in every bed for supporting circulation and immune function, while mint gets a container of its own so it cannot take over the yard, a fact he links playfully to how easily the mind itself wanders. He also flags echinacea and calendula as slightly harder beginners, needing weeks of cold stratification before they will germinate reliably."}, {"title": "Lemon Balm and the Mother Archetype", "body": "The conversation's most extended plant reading centers on lemon balm, botanically Melissa officinalis, named for bees. Chance connects it through biofield tuning to the sacral chakra and an archetypal mother energy, recommending it for anyone carrying frustration, overgiving without receiving nurture, or digestive holding patterns like constipation that trace back to trust issues with a mother figure. James adds that its spreading habit mirrors nourishment given freely, and that pairing it with structure minded herbs balances a household where protection and nurture both matter, since a lack of one can make the other hard to receive."}, {"title": "Preserving the Harvest as Oxymels", "body": "Once herbs are grown, James favors mineral extracted infusions called MLS or oxymels over simple tea, steeping plants in raw apple cider vinegar and honey for a month or more so the acidity pulls out minerals and aromatics without any heat. Their own Mineral Mana blend combines lemon balm, red raspberry, nettle and oat straw specifically for nursing mothers. He suggests diluting a tablespoon in water as a tonic, comparing it to old fashioned switchel, or mixing it fifty fifty with oil for a nutritive salad dressing, framing the whole practice as reestablishing a culture that commercial food replaced."}, {"title": "Horsetail and the Postpartum Transition", "body": "Chance offers an extended biofield reading of horsetail, tying its fast growth and hollow, segmented stalk to impatience and to the sacral chakra's mirror relationship with the pineal gland and third eye. He frames new motherhood as a forced slowdown that clashes with a woman's prior identity built on productivity, and reads horsetail's silica richness for hair, nails and bone as medicine for that transition. James responds that postpartum distress is not a disorder but a signal of missing nutritional, emotional and social support, and that breastfeeding itself shapes a baby's jaw, palate and lifelong breathing and sleep."}]
